1. Core Clinical Tension: A 12-year-old boy presents with severe right lower quadrant abdominal pain, vomiting, high fever, marked leukocytosis, and significantly elevated inflammatory markers, strongly suggesting acute complicated appendicitis with an appendiceal plastron or abscess. However, ultrasonography identifies a large 9-cm septated retrovesical cystic mass, creating diagnostic tension between an atypical complicated appendiceal collection, a pelvic hematoma, and an exceptionally rare primary pelvic hydatid cyst.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs following initial triage blood tests, urinalysis, and abdominal ultrasonography revealing the 9-cm septated retrovesical cystic mass, immediately prior to surgical exploration.
3. Differential Distinctions: An appendiceal plastron or periappendiceal abscess typically manifests as an ill-defined inflammatory mass in direct contiguity with an inflamed appendix, whereas surgical exploration isolated a discrete, encapsulated 10-cm retrovesical cyst. A retrovesical hematoma generally presents following recognized trauma or predisposing coagulopathy and resolves with organized thrombus, whereas this mass was a well-defined cystic lesion containing diagnostic parasitic elements. Notably, indirect hemagglutination was negative, a known pitfall in intact unilocular extrahepatic cysts.
case_prompt: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric emergency department with vomiting and severe abdominal pain. On physical examination, tenderness is elicited in the right lower quadrant. Vital signs demonstrate a body temperature of 37.4°C, pulse rate of 150 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 40 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 105/70 mm Hg. Initial laboratory evaluation reveals a hemoglobin level of 15.4 g/dL and a leukocyte count of 15,600/μL with 55% neutrophils, 40% lymphocytes, and 5% monocytes. Serum creatinine, electrolytes, amylase, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyl transferase concentrations are all within normal limits. The C-reactive protein is markedly elevated at 15.2 mg/dL, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 85 mm/h. Urinalysis shows a specific gravity of 1.020 with positive dipstick reactions for ketones, protein, and blood, but normal microscopic sediment. Abdominal ultrasonography reveals a septated retrovesical cystic mass measuring 9 cm in diameter.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Right lower quadrant tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis in a child strongly suggested complicated acute appendicitis with an inflammatory phlegmon or plastron, but surgical exploration revealed a well-encapsulated, discrete 10-cm retrovesical cystic mass separate from the concurrently inflamed appendix.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: In the differential diagnosis, the patient was considered to be hematoma or plastron to appendicitis and operated on.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A retrovesical hematoma was considered preoperatively given the complex cystic collection on ultrasound, but operative exploration demonstrated an intact 10-cm cystic mass lacking hemorrhagic debris or coagulated blood.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: In the differential diagnosis, the patient was considered to be hematoma or plastron to appendicitis and operated on.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Total surgical excision of the retrovesical cyst and appendectomy, followed by histopathological examination, definitively demonstrated the pathognomonic diagnostic features of a hydatid cyst coexisting with acute appendicitis, despite a negative indirect hemagglutination serology.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Histo-pathologic examinations showed the features of hydatid cyst and appendicitis (Fig. 3). Based on these findings, the diagnosis of hydatid cyst and appendicitis was verified, and treatment of albendazole was initiated.

editor_comments: Primary retrovesical hydatid cyst is an extraordinarily rare presentation of Echinococcosis (accounting for <0.5% of cases) that can clinically mimic acute complicated appendicitis in pediatric patients. Serological testing such as indirect hemagglutination is frequently false-negative in isolated, unruptured extrahepatic cysts, making high-resolution cross-sectional imaging and postoperative histopathology critical for definitive diagnosis.
